subtitle.en: Five geese you can see on British fields and estuaries

intro.en:
Winter is goose season. From October, hundreds of thousands of geese arrive from Iceland, Greenland, Svalbard and Siberia, and the fields and estuaries of Britain fill with the sound of them. If you hear a wild, honking chorus overhead, look up: geese fly in lines and V-shapes, called skeins.

Geese are easier than you think. Each of these five has one detail that gives it away: a black neck with a white chinstrap, a pink bill, a white face. We start with the one you have probably already seen on a park pond.

At the end there's a quiz of eight questions, with birds from the last two weeks mixed in.

explain.en: The front part of the wing. Easy to see in flight.
A white band from cheek to cheek, under the chin.

look_for.en: Big, with a long black neck

where_when.en: Park lakes, reservoirs and farmland all year, all over the country. Brought here from North America as an ornamental bird, in the 1600s.

describe.en: A loud, nasal "ah-honk", and a lot of it.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: It is not a winter visitor but a resident, so you can practise on it any time of the year.

look_for.en: Big and grey-brown, with a thick neck

where_when.en: Lakes and fields, in flocks. Our only native goose that nests here, though many on park lakes are semi-tame. In winter, thousands more arrive from Iceland.

describe.en: The farmyard goose of old: a loud, cackling "aang-ung-ung".

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: The farmyard goose is a descendant of the Greylag.

look_for.en: Smaller and darker than a Greylag, with a dark brown head
Short bill, pink band in the middle

where_when.en: Estuaries and stubble fields in eastern England, Lancashire and Scotland, from October to March. At dawn they leave the roost in huge skeins, with a babble of calls.

describe.en: High, quick, nasal "wink-wink" calls, from a whole flock at once.

chosen.type: call, flight call, nocturnal flight call

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: Most Pink-footed Geese in Britain breed in Iceland and Greenland, and come here for the winter.

dont_confuse.en: Greylag (just before): a bigger, paler goose with an orange bill.

look_for.en: White face, black neck and breast
Small, with a short black bill

where_when.en: Grassy estuaries and islands, mostly on the Solway Firth and Islay in winter. Some feral birds now live on park lakes.

describe.en: A yapping, dog-like "wuk-wuk-wuk", from a big flock.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: In the Middle Ages people thought these geese grew out of barnacles on driftwood. That is how they got their name.

look_for.en: Small, only a little bigger than a Mallard
Black head, neck and breast, with a small white neck patch
Dark body with a white rear end

where_when.en: Muddy estuaries and saltmarshes on the south and east coast, from October to March. They graze on eelgrass and seaweed.

describe.en: A low, rolling "rronk, rronk", from a flock out on the mud.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: The dark-bellied birds here come from Siberia. A paler, light-bellied form winters in Ireland and at Lindisfarne; we leave that one for later.

text.en: Look at the bill and the head. Greylag: big, heavy orange bill and a pale head. Pink-footed: smaller, with a dark head and a short bill with just a pink band. Both have pink legs.

outside.en: Go and look at the geese near you: a park lake, a reservoir or the estuary. Find the Canada Goose first. If you are near the coast, try to be there at dawn or dusk, when the skeins fly.
